This year’s Rising bows to economic realities with a sparser program, but the result is more intimate as it invites greater audience engagement.

Any city arts festival is a curious beast, a Frankensteinian stitching together of commercial, aesthetic and institutional imperatives that only occasionally meld harmoniously. Australian cultural history is littered with the bodies of artistic directors who took the local burghers at their word when they claimed to want “the best of the arts” adorning their cities, only to find with pained surprise that “the best” was often more challenging – and expensive – than they expected.

Rising, an often-tricky amalgam of White Night Melbourne and Melbourne International Arts Festival, is the newest festival to navigate these murky waters. This year, what artistic director Hannah Fox diplomatically describes as a “tighter financial environment” has led to a visibly smaller program.

The emphasis is squarely on dance and an extensive music program. Although they are still present, other art forms are sparse. Perhaps as a result of the tighter focus, this year’s Rising felt more “festivally” than it has recently. One of the hallmarks of a successful festival is a sense of excitement among audience members that floats above the events and intensifies as it progresses.

I felt this strongly during the first week: strangers talked to each other about what they had just seen or were going to see, audiences gathered in clots outside venues after shows having animated conversations. It’s intangible and deeply subjective, an unmeasurable metric that won’t satisfy those who see “success” only as a bottom line, but it was heartening to witness and experience.

Rising now hosts the Australian Dance Biennale, an evolution of Melbourne’s Dance Massive, a two-yearly event that showcased contemporary Australian dance from 2009 to 2019. The biennale offers a feast of Australian and international choreographers, from independent local stalwarts such as Lucy Guerin and Carly Sheppard to Irish choreographer Oona Doherty.

At Chunky Move Studio, Gideon Obarzanek’s exquisite solo dance Glow (2006) was one of two works from the early 2000s remounted for the festival. When it launched, Glow was at the cutting edge of technological design: in collaboration with Obarzanek, German artist Frieder Weiss devised revolutionary motion-tracking lighting that responded to the dancer’s movements – a technique picked up for Kylie Minogue’s 2010 music video “Get Outta My Way”. Technology has moved on, but Glow has lost nothing of its power.

I saw the work’s original dancer, Sara Black (other performances were danced by Melissa Pham and Layla Meadows). The set reflects Obarzanek’s brilliance in establishing spaces that create connections with the audience – the stage is a white square set in boxing-ring seating that creates immediate intimacy and also guarantees there’s not a bad seat in the house.

The dance begins as white lines of laser light pulse ominously across the stage before Black, clothed in a simple white costume, scrabbles into sight. For much of the performance she seems post-human, some strange aquatic creature who is in control of the light’s rigid geometries but also caged by them. The most powerful sequences are those where the dancer struggles with her shadow: it’s still astonishing when she lifts from the floor and her shadow remains behind, coalescing into a demonic blob that stalks her across the stage.

Branch Nebula’s compelling Exposure couldn’t be more of a contrast. Performed by Latai Taumoepeau and Mirabelle Wouters, with sound design from Phil Downing, it’s a visceral, sometimes erotic and often disturbing encounter with the detritus of domesticity.

There’s something in the zeitgeist that demands the spillage of interiority, the refusal of borders, a corporeal rebellion.

Taumoepeau and Wouters are women in their 50s who bring a rich corporeal presence and sardonic wit to their surreal tableaux. The set seems to be sponsored by Bunnings by way of Savers: it features various battered whitegoods (a microwave, a washing machine), a metal bed frame, an old LP player and acres of reflective foil insulation and clear plastic sheets.

These humble objects are deployed in various unexpected ways – the sheets become monsters animated by the performers, or the components of a giant fetish doll, or simply the floor covering of a makeshift stage, while the bed frame becomes a strange lover. Exposure enacts a continual struggle between the performers and the objects they manipulate. It ultimately becomes a cry of protest against – and liberation from – the domestic objects and wider ideologies that imprison and define them. There are many moments of dark comedy, such as when Wouters puts her head in the microwave, but how the work makes its meanings – or opens spaces for these meanings to be made – is less traceable.

Brian Lipson’s work about the Victorian scientist and inventor Frances Galton, A Large Attendance in the Antechamber (2000), is the other remount of the festival. Lipson is not only a consummate actor: he’s one of Australia’s most interesting theatre-makers, specialising in intricately designed and written meta-theatrical shows that excavate the shadows of the personal and social subconscious. This show enjoyed a long life of performances around the world before Lipson retired it in 2007. Two decades later, in a darker time, Lipson brings this grotesque and complex scientist back for another round. “Round” seems apposite, since the show is a combat between the avatar of Galton and the actor who summons him.

Galton, a cousin of Charles Darwin, was a major scientist of his time: among other things, he invented the dog whistle and the forensic use of fingerprints. His main “achievement” was the invention – or at least the elaboration – of the pseudoscience of eugenics, which seeks to create a white master race by eliminating so-called imperfections from humankind. In Galton’s sights was the “inferior” human, especially Black people and those with disability. He was, in other words, an exemplary Victorian colonialist. The shadow of his influence is still potent: as Lipson says in the program, “I feel the cold touch of Galton’s ghost every time I turn to the news.”

The set, a tiny box stuffed with arcane props, is as claustrophobia-inducing as the subject. Galton is supposedly delivering a lecture, although it’s really a series of divagations and interruptions that cumulatively expose the entanglement of so-called “civilisation” with madness and barbarism. Lipson has made some changes: this iteration feels more confronting, as he inhabits Galton as a “self-hating Jew”. This Galton – arrogant, superficially urbane, casually misogynist and racist, skating on the edges of his own sanity – is, like the man who performs him, painfully human.

Perhaps Rising’s biggest coup was programming Austrian choreographer/theatre-maker Florentina Holzinger just as she hit Instagram fame at the Venice Biennale. Although A Year Without Summer is vastly different in scale, its preoccupations are not very far from those in Exposure: the exposed and excessive female body, how women are confined, abused and categorised, how they resist. There’s something in the zeitgeist that demands the spillage of interiority, the refusal of borders, a corporeal rebellion.

It’s the second time I’ve seen Holzinger’s work and it persuades me that she is a consummate artist of our time. Her exhilarating art responds fully to the nightmare of the present: not only in its dystopianism, its knitting of the barbarous past to the horrors of the present, but in the stubborn materiality of its joys.

A Year Without Summer is a musical, albeit one that features Josef Mengele. It also includes an orgiastic Garden of Earthly Delights, perhaps the most to-the-point – and certainly the funniest – critique of Freud’s theories about women’s genitals that I’ve encountered, a heavy-metal takedown of contemporary delusions of immortality, a hospital ward where incontinence gets completely out of control, and many other vignettes including, chillingly, dancing robot dogs.

It sounds chaotic, and it is. It’s also mysteriously coherent, a work that’s made whole by the indomitable presence of the 30 naked women onstage. Their traumas, delights, desires, vulnerabilities and resistances become ours: we trust them to carry us. Tenderly – it’s surprising how tender this show is – they negotiate us through intolerable human realities. If I have to live in this world, I’m glad Holzinger and her cast are there to help us bear it.

Rising continues until June 8.
